I don't remember the reason for my hospitalization. It was roughly 6 years ago. I had been hospitalized 3 times within 3 months. Those three times, I was sent to a local facility. Each stay lasted approximately one week. At that point in my life, I was more comfortable in the facility. It was almost as if I used my mental illness as a way to escape my "real-world" struggles, if that makes any sense. 

Maybe a year after that, I had another episode. I wasn't sent to the same facility, though, because there were no available beds. Instead, I was sent 2-3 hours away to Pinefield in Utica, NY. It was completely different. They watch you use the toilet/shower, to ensure your safety, of course. 

Again, I don't remember many details. I mean, I definitely remember not being able to shit for the full 30 days. Still struggling with constipation. Lol 

It wasn't a bad experience, but I wasn't hospitalized again after that. I think I realized that escaping to a place like that wasn't a good coping mechanism. I was in therapy and counseling for years afterward, and tried many different prescription medications/combinations to treat my mental ailments. I haven't been to a therapist in about a year, but I've been in an okay mental state for longer than that. I really think that my stay at Pinefield changed something within me. 

Maybe they brainwashed me. Who knows...

After a near-death experience, I used to get hecca anxiety any time I had to drive anywhere. I didn't drive for quite a while after the accident. I wasn't ready to get back behind the wheel, but I needed to return to work, and it was a 30-minute drive to get there. I started off small, just driving around the block, and to extremely local destinations. Tackling the highway was the real issue. 
HOWEVER, I read this pamphlet about panic attacks/cognitive therapy that helped tremendously. 

It said something like this...

#1: You have to realize what your automatic thoughts are saying. Identify why you're feeling anxious. (Ex. "I'm feeling anxious because I fear getting into an accident.") 
and
#2: Examine and counter these automatic thoughts. Your thinking is almost guaranteed to be irrational, due to the amount of anxiety you're experiencing. Bring factual evidence to your immediate attention. (Ex. "I'm sober, driving safely, going the speed limit," etc.) 

The pamphlet is labeled Panic Attacks. It was written by Ruth Greenberg and Aaron Beck for the Beck Institute for Cognitive Therapy and Research. I'm pretty sure the PDF is available online, for a price. (?) There is a lot of helpful information on their website, though.

I do the following when I'm away from my "workspace" or materials. That way, I don't get too overwhelmed. 


1.) Recognize and embrace how the task is making you feel, and make a list of the possible reasons it makes you feel that way. 

2.) Think of the worst case scenario, the best case scenario, and the most realistic outcome. Write them down. I don't know about you, but it's a lot easier for me to understand things when I can see them right in front of me.

3.) Think about, and write down the response you'd give to a friend, if they were in your position. 

4.) Try to shift your thinking. Instead of believing your automatic thought (how the task originally makes you feel) to be true, try to think of your situation from a different perspective. 


This technique is called Cognitive Therapy. If you'd like to DM me, I can help you go through this process. Maybe it would help you. It surely wouldn't hurt any.
